Early Shadows: Growing Up with Unseen Pain.
You know, we often think of childhood as this golden time—full of innocence and simple joys. But for some, there’s a quiet ache that just never lets up. Imagine being a young girl in the 1970s, where the days are filled with the usual routines—school, family, friends—but underneath it all, there’s a sadness that lingers. Not the kind that fades with a hug or a favorite treat. This is a heaviness that makes even the happiest moments feel distant, like they belong to someone else.
On the outside, her life might have seemed pretty normal. Parents who argued sometimes, a home that could feel safe one minute and uncertain the next, and the everyday struggle of trying to fit in at school. But deep down, she always felt different—like she was watching life from the sidelines, never quite able to join in. Happiness seemed easy for everyone else, but for her, it felt just out of reach.
At school, she’d watch her classmates laugh and joke around, wondering why joy seemed to come so naturally to them. Sure, teachers would notice her smarts, but they’d also see her drifting off into daydreams, or quietly wiping away tears. And at home, things weren’t much easier. Her mom was always trying to keep things together, but the stress showed. Her dad was distant—sometimes loving, sometimes unpredictable—which only made her crave his approval even more. The constant tension in the house just made her feel more alone.
As she got older, the sadness didn’t disappear. If anything, it got more complicated. She learned how to hide it, to put on a brave face so no one would worry. But inside, that emptiness grew. It became clear that this wasn’t just a phase or a simple reaction to tough family moments. It was something deeper, something she couldn’t quite explain or fix.
Most people around her didn’t see what was really going on. They saw a bright, sensitive kid who sometimes seemed moody or distant. When she tried to talk about what she was feeling, the words never seemed to match the depth of her pain. Well-meaning adults would tell her to cheer up, try harder, or just look on the bright side. But instead of helping, those words just made her feel even more alone.
Back then, mental health just wasn’t something people talked about—especially when it came to kids. Depression didn’t have a name in her world. If you were deeply sad, it was brushed off as being dramatic or attention-seeking. That kind of dismissal made her feel invisible, like her pain was her own fault, not a real struggle.
As she moved into her teenage years, things only got tougher. She started searching for ways to numb the ache—through music, writing, and sometimes even self-destructive habits. These coping tools gave her a little relief, but they never really touched the root of what she was feeling. The world seemed to demand strength and resilience, but she felt herself slipping further away from the person she wanted to become.
Looking back now, it’s clear those early years were shaped by a battle that went way beyond the usual ups and downs of growing up. The seeds of depression had been planted long before she even knew what to call them. And here’s something important to remember: for so many people, mental illness doesn’t start with one big, dramatic event. It’s often a slow, steady wearing away of hope. The journey ahead would be about understanding, surviving, and eventually learning how to live with that darkness that had always been a part of her world.
